Intraocular parasites can give rise to a variety of clinical
signs, predominantly uveitis and secondary glaucoma. 1
Management depends on their identiﬁcation and removal.
Here the parasite was not visible, although ﬁndings from
the referring clinician and clinical signs pointed to nem-
atode-induced uveitis. The patient was a vegetarian, and
we assume she contracted the infection during routine
bathing in a river.
UBM can image areas not easily visualized, such as the
ciliary body, pars plana, and posterior chamber.
2 We have
used it to identify caterpillar setae in unilateral recalcitrant
uveitis.
3 It has been used to image a clinically visible
nematode on the iris surface. 4 In the case described here,
we used it to locate the nematode by both its morphology
and motility, allowing for diagnosis and appropriate
management.

Downbeating Nystagmus and Muscle
Spasms in a Patient with Glutamic-
acid Decarboxylase Antibodies
Beau M. Ances, MD, PhD,
Josep O. Dalmau, MD, PhD,
Jean Tsai, MD, PhD,
M. Josh Hasbani, MD, PhD, and
Steven L. Galetta, MD
PURPOSE:To report the ophthalmic ﬁndings and response
to treatment in a patient with glutamic-acid decarboxyl-
ase antibodies.
DESIGN:Case report.
METHODS: A 55-year-old woman developed progressive,
painful, low back muscle spasms, vertical diplopia, down-
beating nystagmus, and asymmetric appendicular ataxia.
RESULTS:Downbeating nystagmus was present in primary
gaze with an alternating skew deviation in lateral gaze.
Serum and cerebrospinal ﬂuid GAD antibodies were
detected. Treatment with diazepam led to resolution of
spasticity, whereas repeated courses of intravenous im-
munoglobulin improved cerebellar function, including
appendicular ataxia and downbeating nystagmus.
Accepted for publication Dec 14, 2004.

CONCLUSIONS: Patients with GAD antibodies may have
elements of both Stiff-person syndrome (muscle rigidity and
spasms) and prominent cerebellar dysfunction. Treatment
with diazepam rapidly improved Stiff-person symptoms,
whereas IVIg was partially effective at the early stage of
cerebellar dysfunction. (Am J Ophthalmol 2005;140:
142-144. © 2005 by Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.)
G
LUTAMIC ACID DECARBOXYLASE (GAD) CATALYZES
the conversion of glutamate to /H9253-aminobutyric acid
(GABA). The GAD65 isoform may be associated with
insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and other autoim-
mune disorders.
1 Much less frequently, GAD antibodies
are found in patients with Stiff-person syndrome 2 or
cerebellar dysfunction. Previous literature has primarily
focused on the general neurologic features observed with
elevated GAD antibodies with little emphasis on the
neuro-opthalmic ﬁndings.
3 We present a patient who had
ocular ﬁndings due to cerebellar dysfunction and Stiff-
person syndrome with varying responses to treatment.
A 55-year-old woman with a history of IDDM, hyper-
tension, hypothyroidism, and gastroesophageal reﬂux dis-
ease presented with a 4-week course of lower back muscle
spasms, diplopia, and gait difﬁculties. On examination she
had downbeating nystagmus of moderate amplitude and
frequency in primary gaze. An alternating inferior rectus
skew deviation was evident with a right hypertropia in
right lateral gaze and a left hypertropia in left lateral gaze.
She also had minimally increased tone in all extremities
and signiﬁcant dysmetria and appendicular ataxia on the
left. Cerbrospinal ﬂuid examination showed a white blood
cell count of 6 cells/ml and a minimally elevated protein
value of 61 mg/dl. Studies for known paraneoplastic
antibodies (including Anti-Yo, Hu, Ma1, Ma2, Ri, CV2/
CRMP5) were negative. GAD antibodies were detected in
both the serum and CSF using immunohistochemistry and
radioimmunoanalysis (Figure 1). Brain magnetic resonance
imaging was normal with no Arnold-Chiari malformation
observed. Brain ﬂuoro-deoxyglucose positron emission to-
mography was also unremarkable. Computed tomography
scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis were normal.
The patient was treated with diazepam and intravenous
methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days), which resulted in
improvement in her muscle spasm but no change in her
other symptoms. Subsequently, she received intravenous
immunoglobulin (IVIg, 0.4 gm/kg/day) for 5 days, and a

signiﬁcant reduction in nystagmus, and a reduction in
dysmetria were noted.
The neuro-opthalmic ﬁndings in our patient are most
likely due to cerebellar dysfunction and the effect of GAD
antibodies on GABAergic transmission.
4 Lesions within the
posterior midline of the cerebellum may produce downbeat-
ing nystagmus.
5 We know of no other studies that fully
describe the neuro-opthalmic consequences of GAD antibod-
ies. As demonstrated by this case, patients with GAD
antibodies may have elements of both Stiff-person syndrome
(muscle rigidity and spasms) and prominent cerebellar dys-
function. Treatment with diazepam may rapidly improve Stiff-
person symptoms, whereas IVIg may allow for improvement in
cerebellar dysfunction, including downbeat nystagmus.

Displacement of Rectus Muscle
Pulleys by Torsional Muscle Surgery
for Treatment of Full Macular
Translocation-induced Incyclotropia
Reika Kono, MD, PhD,
Hiroshi Ohtsuki, MD, PhD,
Hirotaka Okanobu, MD, and
Kazushi Kinugasa, MD, PhD
PURPOSE:To elucidate the coronal plane locations of
extraocular muscle (EOM) pulleys following torsional
muscle surgery.
DESIGN:Case report.
METHODS:A 76-year-old man underwent advancement of
the anterior part of the inferior oblique muscle to treat
full macular translocation–induced incyclotropia. Post-
operatively, magnetic resonance imaging was used to
obtain contiguous, 2-mm-thick coronal orbital images.
On each MRI image, the cross-sectional area and center
of the EOM was computed, and all rectus EOM positions
were translated to the coordinate origin at the area
centroid of the globe at the level of pulleys.
RESULTS: The superior rectus pulley was displaced tem-
porally, and the lateral rectus pulley was displaced infe-
riorly more than 2 SD from normal subjects. Coronal
plane locations of EOM pulleys of the ipsilateral eye
showed extorsion compared with that of the contrale-
sional eye.
CONCLUSIONS:Torsional muscle surgery causes an extor-
sional shift of the superior and lateral rectus pulleys.
(Am J Ophthalmol 2005;140:144-146. © 2005 by
Elsevier Inc. All rights reserved.)

AGNETIC RESONANCE IMAGING ALLOWS DIRECT
evaluation of the functional anatomy of extraocular
muscles (EOMs), demonstrating pulleys that have proven
fundamental to every aspect of ocular motility.
1 The coronal
plane location of each rectus pulley is highly uniform in
normal subjects.
1,2 However, the effect of muscle displace-
ment–induced strabismus surgery on pulley positions is un-
known. We report a case showing displacement of rectus

pulleys after torsional muscle surgery
3 to treat full macular
translocation (FMT)–induced incyclotropia.4
Since 1990, a 76-year-old man demonstrated cyclover-
tical diplopia after FMT to treat age-related macular
degeneration. The patient slit-beam test demonstrated
/H1101120 –25 degree incyclodeviation before torsional muscle
surgery. The anterior portion of the inferior oblique muscle
was advanced 16 mm in March 2001, correcting the
incyclodeviation to almost zero. Orbital MRI with high-
resolution T
1-weighted imaging was performed using Gen -
eral Electric Sigma 1.5 T scanner after strabismus surgery. 3
Imaging was performed quasicoronally in central gaze. On
each digital MRI image, the center of the relevant EOM
was computed using the “X-Y center” function of the NIH
Image program (W. Rasband, National Institutes of
Health). To normalize position on the scan plane, all
rectus EOM positions were analyzed at 9 mm posterior to
the globe center, that is, inferred pulley locations.
Figure 1 shows the horizontal line passing through the
center of the medial rectus at the level of pulleys. The
ipsilateral lateral rectus was located inferior to the hori-
zontal line compared with that of the contralateral eye.
